title: Alfie
full_review:
Many will ask how anyone could dare remake the famous 1966 British film which, more than any other, put Michael Caine so memorably on the map. But Charles Shyer's New York-set "Alfie" (Paramount) works just as well on its own terms, capped by a superb performance by Jude Law in the title role. His frequent monologues delivered to the camera are deliciously entertaining.

Many who cry foul that they would dare remake a classic forget that "Alfie" was first a play in London's West End and then on Broadway with Adam Faith and Terence Stamp, respectively.
Alfie is an unapologetic womanizer who -- as confirmed by his addresses to the camera -- relishes each new conquest. There's his more-or-less steady girlfriend, a good-natured single mom (Marisa Tomei); an unhappy housewife (Jane Krakowski); an anything-goes party girl (Sienna Miller) whom he callously drops, even after she straightens out her life; a wealthy matron (Susan Sarandon, looking more like Bette Davis with each film); and Lonette (Nia Long), the girlfriend of his best friend (Omar Epps).
Law's back-seat limo encounter with Krakowski may be the most graphic sex scene in the film, but the one with Sarandon is the most sensual.

A cancer scare briefly pulls him up short, and he begins to reflect on life's true values. (Tony Award-winner Jefferson Mays from Broadway's "I Am My Own Wife" has a scene-stealing turn as an effeminate doctor.) But as soon as he's given a clean bill of health, he slips back to his randy ways.

Eventually, though, matters take a serious turn when he has a fling with Lonette, the girlfriend of his fellow limo driver, Marlon. Lonette confides in him that she's pregnant, and he takes her to have a presumed abortion. When she emerges, she poignantly tells him she feels empty.

Alfie's callous ways eventually turn sour, and he finds himself having to re-examine his whole life, as he finds himself unattached, but with no peace of mind. "If you don't have that, you have nothing," he muses.

Law is wonderfully affecting in this transformation -- and indeed, if memory serves, plays Alfie more sympathetically than Caine did. The emptiness of his hedonistic lifestyle is beautifully conveyed as the story progresses. The result is a cautionary tale of the first order.

The women are all perfectly cast. The Americanization of the story all around takes nothing from the original, and the contemporary spin is sensitively done.

There's a marvelous cameo from Dick Latessa, as an older widower who knows a thing or two about life and love and gives Alfie some good, common-sense advice ("think before unzipping," he says bluntly).

The music is by Mick Jagger and Dave Stewart. But yes, the famous Burt Bacharach theme song -- originally sung by Cher, though Dionne Warwick had the chart hit -- is used discreetly before the opening credits and at the very end, but, otherwise, this is a quite fresh take on a well-remembered property, done with great style.

Because of some rough and crude language, strong sexual content, nudity and recreational drug use, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
